summary: Kitchenham-style review of AI/NLP test-case generation from natural-language requirements (2000 to Oct 2025): 26 primary studies (21 from the PRISMA flow plus 5 from a later supplementary search), nine of them LLM-based. It groups work into formalism, statistical-NLP and hybrid/LLM eras, codes eight hand-picked studies Low/Medium/High on six criteria, and concludes that no approach is simultaneously automated, ambiguity-robust, domain-broad, traceable, well evaluated and hallucination-controlled. It proposes a test-generation hallucination benchmark, a requirements-to-test traceability matrix pipeline, a complexity-stratified benchmark and on-premises deployment blueprints, none of which are built.

claims.claim: No existing approach satisfies all six quality dimensions
claims.evidence: Table IV codes only 8 purposively selected studies with the authors' own Low/Medium/High judgments; no second coder or agreement statistic; criteria defined after reading the corpus. With 8 studies and 6 trade-off-laden criteria, the result is close to guaranteed.

claims.claim: Formal traceability is traded for input flexibility: only controlled-input or model-based approaches produce requirements-to-test traceability, and fully generative LLM studies produce none
claims.evidence: §VI-D gap finding 1 and §VII-B: NAT2TESTSCR/CPN and UMTG yield traceability artifacts; CiRA keeps partial links; the LLM studies listed report none. Plausible corpus-level observation, but the corpus has only nine LLM studies and stops at Oct 2025.

claims.claim: Effective hallucination control requires external anchoring (formal layers, cause-effect graphs, retrieval)
claims.evidence: Inferred from the authors' own K6 ratings; the quantitative support is HaluEval (general QA, not test generation) and a 10-document GPT-4 vs Mistral-7B correctness gap, which measures model capability rather than hallucination or anchoring.

claims.claim: Test-generation accuracy degrades with requirement complexity
claims.evidence: Medeshetty et al.: rule-based extraction 95% -> 75% -> 60% by signal count; Korraprolu et al.: six LLMs at most 50.2% MCDC vs ~79% decision coverage. The survey also cites the GPT-4/Mistral-7B gap on identical inputs as a complexity effect, which it is not.

claims.claim: The survey is the first focused, LLM-era-inclusive synthesis of NL-requirements-to-test generation
claims.evidence: The core query ANDs three exact phrases ('Test Case Generation', 'Artificial Intelligence', 'Natural Language Requirements'); 5 qualifying studies were missed by it and added later; only nine LLM-based studies are included, CiRA (RoBERTa extraction) is counted among them, and §VI-A is titled 'twenty-one' while analyzing twenty-six.

patterns.note: Secondary synthesis, no comparison of its own: structured inputs (CNL, EARS/Rupp boilerplates, RUCM use cases, acceptance criteria) enable deterministic, traceable test derivation in primary studies (UMTG, NAT2TEST, SPECMATE 56% and CiRA 71.8% of manual tests generated in industry) but restrict authoring, and boilerplate extraction falls to 10% on one PURE dataset.

Recommendation R2 proposes an auditable requirements-to-test traceability matrix pipeline; nothing is implemented or evaluated. Reports that no fully generative LLM study in its corpus emits a traceability artifact.
Calls for a test-generation hallucination benchmark and a complexity-stratified benchmark; neither is built.
Formal back-ends (SCR tables, Coloured Petri Nets, OCL constraint solving) appear as the anchoring layer in the most traceable primary studies.

methodology.sample: 26 primary studies (539 records -> 136 full texts -> 21 included, plus 5 from a supplementary search outside the PRISMA flow); Table IV codes 8
methodology.models: n/a; primary studies span GPT-3.5/4, Gemini, Claude, LLaMA-3, Mistral, fine-tuned GPT-3.5
methodology.variance: n/a; no inter-coder agreement for screening, quality scoring or six-criterion coding
methodology.languages: Requirements mostly English (one bilingual German/English study); target test languages vary

standards.artifacts: Search string and PRISMA counts given; no extraction sheet, per-study quality scores or coding data released

biases.detail: Central gap analysis uses 8 purposively chosen studies; the authors assert but do not show that the full corpus agrees.
26 studies over 25 years, nine LLM-based; narrow exact-phrase search.
Compares incommensurable metrics (business-scenario coverage, mutation score, OCL accuracy, coverage) to argue a common ceiling; uses general-QA HaluEval rates for test-generation hallucination.
'First', 'evidence-based', 'strict' framing for a subjective single-team coding exercise.

verdict_reason: Usable as a pointer list to primary studies (UMTG, CiRA, SPECMATE, RAGTAG, LLM4Fin), but the search is narrow, LLM-era coverage is thin, the headline gap matrix is a subjective coding of 8 hand-picked studies with no second coder, and the hallucination argument leans on non-test-generation evidence. Low weight.
applicability: For pre-spec clarification, the useful pointer is that requirement form decides what can be automated and traced later: requirements written as conditionals or acceptance criteria (EARS, cause-effect, Gherkin) yielded tests with links back to requirement IDs in industrial studies, while free-text-to-LLM pipelines produced tests with no link back. A discovery harness should therefore push clarified requirements into structured, ID-bearing form that tests and code can cite. The survey says nothing about discovery, onboarding, Java or multi-repo work, and its LLM coverage ends in Oct 2025.
